answers.label: Benefits and challenges of consequential methods
answers.text:
Consequential accounting currently faces methodological and implementation challenges; however, if carefully designed and transparently applied, it can provide critical, complementary information to attributional inventories.

Current Challenges:

• Optional, rarely used today; often absent or a low priority within target- and goal-setting programs and disclosures.

• Non-standardized methodology often viewed as not actionable. Survey feedback indicated clear need to enable new usable methods and metrics for how to quantify and report GHG impacts.

• Forecast models based on assumptions and hypothetical baselines aren’t fact-based and vulnerable to gaming. Demonstrating additionality is difficult to define with likely false positives and negatives.

• Credibility concerns – poorly designed claims can be conflated with non-verifiable, “low-quality” carbon offsets, undermining trust.

Potential Benefits:

• Add essential, complementary information. Inventories allocate the "emissions pie" (responsibility), while consequential accounting determines if the pie is shrinking or expanding (impact). Survey feedback highlighted both inventory and consequential methods are essential and complementary to drive ambition and achieve meaningful decarbonization targets. They’re different calculations with different purposes. The Protocol recognizes there’s a gap between reported inventory emissions and real-world climate impact.

• Address recognized challenges with Project accounting by providing clear standardized methods and actionable guidance for consequential accounting and improved environmental reporting. Estimating grid-level impacts, even if imperfectly, is vital for making better investment, procurement, and consumption decisions.

• Encourage high-impact decisions. New impact disclosures can identify and prioritize (discourage) procurement and consumption actions that reduce (or increase) system-level emissions.

o They can prioritize investments in incremental CFE, emerging technologies, PPA off-take, extending the operating lives of existing CFE, etc.
o Impact metrics also enable meaningful climate actions limited by more granular MBM (e.g., providing alternatives for companies without local supply options, investing beyond clean grids, investing in Global South, capturing economies of scale for PPAs when not enough load exists to finance new generation locally).
o Since many companies operate globally, impact estimates can help prioritize procurement and consumption actions across and within market areas to achieve inventory reductions with greater impact.
o Impact metrics can be used to recognize that not all EACs, even if additional, have the same climate benefit.
o Impact metrics are needed to both maintain and expand the accessibility of climate-beneficial decisions, to determine how to spend climate dollars wisely, and let companies choose where, when, and what resources to procure for greatest climate effect.

• Protect credibility and relevance of GHG reporting. Stakeholders want to estimate carbon impact and have criticized GHGP for failing to connect disclosures with actual emissions reductions. Absent any required impact accounting, it’ll be possible to significantly increase emissions to the atmosphere while reporting low or zero MB emissions, which will erode the credibility, scientific integrity, and relevance of GHG reporting.

Potential Risks / Unintended Consequences:

• Repeat fundamental problems with Project accounting status quo (current challenges).

• Jeopardize feasibility at scale, making it unable to provide decision-useful information, if non-standardized methods, optional reporting, and “too” stringent additionality tests are required.

• Ignore or underestimate significant harms (e.g., new fossil build tied to new load) if only avoided emissions and Scope 2 inventories are reported.

answers.label: Appropriateness of the TWG subgroup formula
Why the formula is or is not appropriate
answers.text:
While the public consultation survey refers to the “proposed Scope 2 TWG subgroup formula,” several critical elements of the proposal are not reflected in the consultation materials. As presented, the formula in the consultation doesn’t achieve the core objectives of the marginal impact proposal. Authors of the subgroup formula have publicly identified several material differences:

1) Core calculation: The public consultation focuses only on avoided emissions from projects outside corporate inventories. It doesn’t capture the grid-level emission impacts of electricity consumption or procurement actions that increase emissions (e.g., contracting with fossil resources). In contrast, the subgroup's proposal explicitly quantifies both emissions caused by electricity consumption and emissions avoided (or caused) by procurement actions within and outside inventory boundaries. Including both elements provides a more complete, comparable, and decision-relevant picture of system-level impacts and supports more effective abatement planning, offering insights not reflected in LBM or MBM reporting. Without both metrics, avoided emissions can’t be meaningfully interpreted or compared, particularly when companies increase load in high-marginal emissions locations or hours. The consultation materials also fail to address energy storage, which both consumes and discharges electricity, and therefore requires both effects to be measured under a consequential approach.

2) Required vs. optional reporting: The public consultation doesn’t indicate whether consequential metrics related to electricity consumption and procurement would be required alongside LB and MB inventories. The subgroup proposal explicitly required reporting of these metrics, recognizing that optional, non-prioritized disclosures are unlikely to influence behavior or improve decision-making.

3) Lack of standardized methodology: The consultation doesn’t propose a standardized method for calculating consequential impacts. By contrast, the subgroup developed a detailed, electricity-specific methodology based on observable, historical data rather than forecasts or speculative modeling assumptions, improving transparency, comparability, and auditability.

4) Treatment of additionality: The consultation lists potential additionality tests for general feedback but doesn’t show how they would be applied in practice. The subgroup proposal introduced a structured, two-step approach requiring projects to meet impact quality criteria (e.g., regulatory, timing, and financial or positive-list tests) and to demonstrate impact relative to a standardized baseline.

5) Intended application: The consultation materials are positioned as input to broader, sector-agnostic AMI TWG work across all scopes. The subgroup's proposal developed by electricity experts focused on delivering near-term, actionable recommendations to advance consequential accounting within the Scope 2 Guidance for the electricity sector, including clear methodologies and guidance for calculation, with the potential to expand to other scopes and sectors over time.

As a result, the public consultation doesn’t present a concrete proposal for implementing a consequential accounting standard for electricity. Absent such a proposal, the fundamental shortcomings of the current Project Protocol – its lack of standardization, limited use, and weak decision relevance – remain unresolved. Electricity has unique physical, market system, and accounting characteristics that require sector-specific methods. If consequential approaches continue to be non-standardized, optional, and unsuitable for target-setting, serious concerns will persist regarding the Protocol’s relevance, credibility, and scientific integrity. Ultimately, if reporters can omit actions that materially increase emissions or present misleading claims about climate impact, the Protocol will fail where it matters most, enabling real reductions in emissions to the atmosphere.

answers.label: Secondary effects to consider, and how
answers.text:
My response depends on whether build margin, incorporated in the proposed baseline-setting procedure, is considered a secondary effect.

(NOTE: As explained in Chapter 5 of the Project Protocol, the GHG assessment boundary encompasses all the primary effects and significant secondary effects associated with a GHG project and the primary effect is defined as a change relative to baseline emissions. Build margin isn’t specifically addressed in the Project Protocol. As described in Section 2.3 for Grid-Connected Electricity Projects, baseline emissions are calculated using a weighted average
of BM and OM emission factors.)

Build margin is intended to capture longer-run structural changes to the power system that occur as a result of the action, most importantly, changes in investment decisions (what capacity gets built, delayed, or retired). These tend to occur over longer time horizons, depend on broader market and policy responses, and are more indirect than plant dispatch changes. That said, BM effects are still core to consequential accounting. Many credible approaches therefore treat OM as the dominant short-term signal, include BM as a complementary long-term signal, and apply them together (often with standardized weighting) to reflect both near-term and durable system impacts.

To be included, BM must be methodologically robust and standardized. Speculative or assumption heavy secondary effects should be optional and not included in required routine GHG disclosures (see response to Q. 23).

In sum, both OM and BM should be required using a standardized methodology, while complex or speculative secondary effects (like life-cycle emissions) may be reported on an optional basis.

Furthermore, some actions, like installing carbon capture on a fossil plant or accelerating the retirement of a fossil plant (i.e., the one-time effect of decommissioning and termination
of a project activity), may also require special treatment. Carbon capture or early plant retirement can result in direct abatement of fossil emissions associated with a specific plant and/or affect how the plant is operated that may not be fully reflected in the OM or BM impact assessment. The emissions impact arises both from the permanent elimination of emissions from a specific unit and from how the system replaces its energy and capacity over time. OM may capture short-term dispatch responses immediately following retirement, while BM may reflect longer-term replacement capacity. However, neither OM nor BM alone fully captures the immediate, irreversible cessation of emissions from the retired plant. Special treatment may therefore be needed to separately recognize: 1) the direct cessation of emissions from the unit (using observed and verifiable data), and 2) the consequential effects associated with replacement generation and capacity decisions. This ensures that consequential accounting appropriately reflects both direct structural changes and broader grid responses.

answers.label: Why secondary effects should be excluded
answers.text:
The scope of any required, routine marginal impact assessment should be limited to primary effects of electricity-sector actions occurring during the reporting period, consistent with how Scope 2 inventories for electricity consumption and procurement are defined and reported (see caveats in response to Q. 22). This boundary is essential to ensure feasibility, auditability, comparability, and alignment with GHGP accounting principles.

1) Alignment with Scope 2 Boundaries: Scope 2 inventories capture direct combustion-related emissions from grid-connected electricity attributable to consumption and procurement, while explicitly excluding upstream life-cycle emissions. Those upstream emissions are addressed in Scope 3, Category 3 (fuel- and energy-related activities). Applying the same boundary to marginal impact accounting ensures conceptual consistency with Scope 2-related consumption and procurement actions.

2) Primary Effects are Attributable and Auditable: Under the Project Protocol, a primary effect is the intended change in GHG emissions, removals, or storage directly caused by a project activity, with each activity generally having one primary effect. Primary effects are directly attributable, observable, and auditable using standardized data. For electricity-sector actions, these primary effects are most appropriately measured as changes in combustion emissions from grid-connected generation, varying by time and location.

3) Consistent Treatment of Consumption, Generation, and Storage: Limiting required reporting to primary effects enables a coherent, internally consistent framework across electricity actions, including:

• Electricity consumption (siting, time-of-use, efficiency, etc.),

• Generation projects meeting defined impact quality criteria (aligned with the type of claims made), and

• Energy storage systems, which must account symmetrically for both charging and discharging impacts.

This approach ensures that both sides of the equation are disclosed – emissions increases (e.g., new load or new fossil generation) and reductions are captured, avoiding the one-sided “avoided-only” framing that undermines current Project accounting. Under this framework, impacts depend on where and when consumption, generation and storage occur, using a consistent methodology.

4) Why Secondary Effects Shouldn’t be Required: Secondary effects often rely on speculative assumptions and forecasts, are difficult to verify, increase the risk of double counting, and reduce comparability across reporters. GHGP recognizes that secondary effects are frequently small and may be excluded. Requiring them for routine reporting would undermine feasibility and likely continue the barriers that have resulted in Project accounting being rarely used and a low priority.

5) Routine Metrics versus Ad Hoc Studies: The marginal impact method (MIM) developed by the Scope 2 TWG subgroup was never intended to replace full consequential analyses that include secondary effects. Those studies remain appropriate for prospective decision-making and policy analysis. Instead, the objective was to provide a standardized, electricity-specific method based on observable, historical data that captures both emissions caused and avoided by consumption, generation, and storage, and can produce decision-useful information reported routinely alongside Scope 2 inventories.

6) Why This Boundary is Necessary: The public consultation doesn’t propose a concrete, standardized method for evaluating secondary effects. Expanding required reporting beyond primary effects without such a method would likely worsen, not solve, the credibility, feasibility, and comparability challenges facing consequential accounting.

Limiting required marginal impact reporting to primary effects strikes the necessary balance between integrity, feasibility, and decision usefulness, while preserving space for more comprehensive consequential analyses where appropriate.

answers.label: Why annual or lifetime reporting
answers.text:
Calculating and reporting emissions impacts each reporting year, rather than estimating impacts once for the full project lifetime, best satisfies the GHG Protocol’s core principles of integrity, accuracy, comparability, feasibility, and decision usefulness.

Like financial statements (balance sheet, income statement, cash flow), GHG reporting should be fact-based, verifiable, and auditable. While long-term forecasts may inform internal planning and investment decisions, external GHG disclosures should rely on objective, empirical evidence of what occurred during the reporting year, consistent with how Scope 2 inventories already report electricity consumption and procurement.

Electricity-sector impacts are inherently time- and location-specific and can change rapidly as grid conditions evolve. The same consumption or procurement action can have materially different emissions impacts across hours, years, or locations – even within the same grid. Unlike MB inventory accounting, where a contract with a CFE generator may yield a constant zero EF for the contract term, the marginal emissions impact of a project can rise or fall over time due to changes in dispatch, grid mix, congestion, policy, or load growth. Lifetime estimates can “lock-in” highly inaccurate impacts for long periods. Scientific integrity is strengthened when reported impacts evolve with actual system conditions rather than remaining fixed based on assumptions made at project inception.

Lifetime impact estimates depend on long-term forecasts, which are inherently uncertain, subjective, and unverifiable. They require assumptions about grid evolution, fuel prices, technology costs, policy trajectories, and dispatch behavior over decades. Different analysts will reasonably reach different conclusions, undermining comparability and creating opportunities for speculation, gaming, and overstatement of benefits. Forecasts are almost always wrong over long horizons and contradict basic accounting principles that emphasize reliability, objectivity, consistency, transparency, and standardization.

These shortcomings help explain why existing project-based accounting approaches, heavily reliant on hypothetical counterfactuals and forecasts, are rarely used and are often a low priority in target-setting and disclosures. There’s broad agreement among Scope 2 TWG members that the status quo Project Protocol isn’t a viable option for routine reporting due to its dependence on speculative assumptions, multiple calculation methodologies, and differing interpretations of additionality.

The objective of the Consequential Subgroup was therefore to provide focused, actionable recommendations for electricity-sector impact accounting, including clear methodologies and guidance, by requiring only “in-year” marginal impacts of consumption and procurement actions in the core calculation, using accessible (public, free, and credible), observable historical data. This approach was never intended to replace ad-hoc, forward-looking lifecycle or system-wide studies, which remain appropriate for internal decision-making or policy analysis and may be disclosed separately on an optional basis.

Annual, ex-post impact reporting improves comparability across projects and reporters, reflects changes in hard-to-predict actual market conditions, prevents gaming of speculative lifetime benefits, and aligns reported impacts with actions taken in each reporting period. By contrast, the public consultation doesn’t provide a clear, standardized methodology for a one-time lifetime impact approach and therefore doesn’t resolve the fundamental shortcomings that have limited the relevance and credibility of consequential accounting to date.

In short, reporting electricity-sector emissions impacts annually based on what actually happened preserves scientific integrity, improves transparency, and produces decision-useful information, while leaving space for broader forward-looking analyses where appropriate.

answers.label: Requiredness of the financial analysis test
Requiredness of the common practice test
Why selected tests should be included
answers.text:
The appropriate treatment of additionality depends on the specific questions being asked, the purpose of the metric, and the claims being supported. Without clearly defining the problem to be solved, agreement on solutions, particularly around additionality, is unlikely.

Whether additionality should be required, and how it should be defined, is one of the most contested issues in GHG accounting. As the Project Protocol (PP) recognizes, there’s no technically “correct” level of stringency; it’s inherently a policy choice (PP, p. 19). There’s no consensus on the validity of any particular test, and accordingly the Project Protocol doesn’t require specific additionality tests (PP, p. 20). Instead, additionality is implicitly addressed through baseline-setting procedures, where interpretation and stringency are left to user discretion (PP, p. 8). High stringency reduces false positives but increases false negatives, potentially discouraging program participation (PP, p. 71). This tradeoff can’t be resolved purely through technical methods.

Current MBM doesn’t require additionality. By design, MBM reflects all generation, old and new, mandated and voluntary, regardless of causation (Guidance, p. 90-91). A key design question for a marginal impact method (MIM) is therefore whether it should reflect only voluntary procurement or all actions that affect grid-level emissions, including those driven by policy mandates. This distinction materially affects applicable tests, supported claims, and feasibility, especially in jurisdictions like the U.S., where most CFE is required under existing or scheduled mandates.

For MIM to be practical and decision-useful, additionality assessments and baseline determinations don’t need to be perfect. They must be credible, consistent, and superior to available alternatives. Impractical and highly subjective causal mapping exercises should be avoided, as they undermine feasibility, auditability and comparability. Strict additionality tests risk moving impact accounting away from fact-based disclosures.

GHGP reporting should prioritize objective, observable, and repeatable disclosures, while incentivizing actions plausibly associated with impact, such as investments in new generation, advanced technologies, long-term PPAs that derisk financing, or other forms of incremental clean energy support. These actions can and should be recognized directly through consistent metrics grounded in real-world procurement practices, rather than through binary additionality claims. GHGP already acknowledges that changes in grid-level emissions often diverge from changes in reported inventories. Rather than omitting this information, fact-based impact disclosures should be required, with claims tailored to what the data substantiates.

Key questions for MIM design include:

1. What decisions is MIM intended to inform? (See responses to Q. 34 and Q. 42.)
2. Did an action occur that affects grid-level emissions? (See response to Q. 30.)
3. Who paid for the action?
4. What combination of actors or forces caused the action? (policy, monopoly supplier decisions, economics, voluntary buyers, etc.) (See response to Q. 29.)
5. What emissions effect did the action have? (See responses to Q. 37, Q. 40 and Q. 41).

Incremental CFE may be paid for by reporters without being caused by them (see SSS discussion). Additionality isn’t binary; different types of purchases may contribute to different levels of additionality. Climate outcomes don’t depend on who claims responsibility (e.g., the climate doesn’t care if emissions are allocated to company A or B’s inventory), but on the magnitude, timing, and location of emissions changes. Experts broadly agree that not all EACs, or even all “additional” resources, have equal climate impact. Designing MIM around these realities enables more accurate, decision-relevant, and credible reporting, without over-relying on subjective additionality tests.

answers.label: Context on test feasibility
answers.text:
There’re valid reasons why the Project Protocol isn’t widely used today, and those reasons should be addressed directly. Absent a specific, actionable, and standardized proposal that relies on accessible, fact-based data to quantify and report GHG impacts, continued focus on abstract additionality concepts risks wasting scarce time and perpetuating the status quo: non-standardized, low-priority reporting that’s unsuitable for target-setting and unable to prioritize actions that reduce actual emissions to the atmosphere.

Quantification methods must be fit for purpose. Tests that rely on forecasts or modeling built on subjective assumptions aren’t feasible for standardized reporting. Methods and data should support intended uses and claims and ensure reported impacts are accurate and not misleading (see responses to Q. 27, Q. 30, Q. 34, and Q. 42).

A core problem is the persistent conflation of actions, causation, and effects. A reporter may cause an action that leads to emissions effects but may take actions without causing them (e.g., complying with policy mandates). Further, actions can have materially different effects depending on context, such as achieving a zero MB inventory in Norway versus India, or in a jurisdiction with a 100% RPS versus one without. Two companies can report identical MB information while the climate impacts of their actions differ substantially.

EACs can serve multiple climate-relevant functions, including supporting new clean energy development, enabling existing clean generation to remain economically viable, reducing reliance on public subsidies/spending (e.g., public subsidies coupled with private payments), and informing policy and tax measures. These functions vary by market and procurement type, and none require binary additionality determinations to be decision-useful.

GHGP’s apparent focus on strict additionality tests to support causal claims is misplaced. While causal attribution is appropriate for some use cases, it’s largely unnecessary for informing decarbonization decisions. At the extreme, reporters could be required to demonstrate they undertook actions no one else would take, potentially because they are excessively costly, inefficient, or unrealistic. Such standards may provide comfort that reporters caused such actions but would fail as climate policy and would not scale the actions needed for decarbonization.

With respect to system-level impacts, GHGP applies inconsistent logic in inventory and consequential accounting.

Scope 2 Guidance:
• Assumes all EAC purchases increase demand, raise prices, stimulate supply, and result in aggregate emissions changes (p. 89)
• Doesn’t require a cause-and-effect relationship between reporter and action (p. 28)
• Considers all consumption and procurement
• Applies to compliance and voluntary actions
• Relies on fact-based, historical data
• Allows the same EAC to yield different inventory reductions depending on who buys it or how it’s applied
• Produces inventory reductions that don’t reflect either short-run or long-run marginal system impacts and may occur without any change in grid emissions.

Consequential:
• Assumes only EACs passing additionality tests affect global emissions
• Requires a demonstrable cause-and-effect relationship
• Ignores consumption and procurement actions that increase emissions
• Restricts applicability to voluntary procurement
• Depends on uncertain, speculative forecasts
• Assigns identical emissions impact to the same EAC regardless of buyer
• Designed to reflect short- and long-run marginal system impacts.

Inconsistent change theories undermine credibility and usability. Rather than doubling down on additionality constructs that have limited project accounting use, GHGP should prioritize standardized, transparent, fact-based impact disclosures that reflect where, when, and how emissions change. Such an approach would better support comparability, target-setting, and real-world decarbonization outcomes.

answers.label: Additionality tests missing from the framework
answers.text:
Environmental claims should be linked to new metrics that identify, differentiate, and incentivize procurement and consumption actions with higher real-world climate impact (see response to Q. 34).

Four points:

1) Incrementality as an Action-Based, Non-Causal Test:

An incrementality test also should be considered to support non-causal environmental claims. This differs from a timing test, which evaluates whether a reporter helped cause investment decisions. Incrementality instead assesses whether a discrete, identifiable action changed system behavior relative to a prior state (e.g., new builds, uprates, life extensions, repowering, or operational dispatch changes). This approach is more compatible with fact-based, auditable reporting because it doesn’t require identifying who caused the action, only that a system-relevant change occurred.

2) Consequential Accounting Shouldn’t be Limited to RE Projects (as stated in Q. 30):

MIM should apply uniformly across all generation technologies (fossil and clean), procurement and consumption actions, interventions that increase or decrease emissions, and compliance-driven and voluntary actions. GHGP already recognizes that Scope 2 inventories often diverge from real-world climate impacts, creating a need for carbon-aware metrics – to assess whether global emissions are rising or falling (changing the size of the “pie”), separate from inventory allocation (dividing the “pie”).

Actions that could be informed by impact-related metrics include:

Consumption:
• Siting or expanding load on grids with available clean supply
• Relocating or reducing load where fossil displacement is possible
• Investing in EE
• Shifting load to cleaner hours.

Procurement:
• Adding incremental resources
• Locating supply to displace high-emitting marginal generation
• Operating existing or new storage to charge clean and discharge when grid is emissions-intensive
• Encouraging fossil retirement or lower-carbon substitutes
• Enabling mitigation for entities on already-clean grids or without local supply options
• Supporting clean energy investment in developing regions, even if operations are elsewhere.

For multi-location companies pursuing MB inventory goals, MIM can help prioritize both compliance and voluntary actions that deliver the greatest reductions in atmospheric emissions.

3) Standardized Baselines:

“Distinguishing a project activity from its baseline scenario is often referred to as determining additionality” (PP, p. 16). All grid-level effects should be measured against standardized baseline-setting procedures to ensure comparability, credibility and feasibility.

4) Tiered Claims Supported by Tiered Tests:

Rather than binary additionality thresholds, different tests, with different thresholds, should support tiered environmental claims aligned with evidentiary strength.

Examples:

Weaker Claims:
• Fail incrementality / fail regulatory test (e.g., EACs from existing resources or SSS)
• Fail incrementality / pass regulatory test (e.g., voluntary EACs from existing resources)
• Pass incrementality / fail regulatory test (e.g., new generation built to meet policy mandates).

Stronger Claims:
• Pass incrementality / pass regulatory test (e.g., voluntary support for new clean generation).

Strongest Claims (Causal):
• Pass timing + regulatory + positive list or financial analysis test (e.g., reporter caused new CFE to be built)
• First-of-a-kind and common practice tests can be incorporated in positive list and financial analysis test approaches as emerging technologies often require greater financial support.

Designing MIM and associated claims around observable actions, standardized baselines, and tiered evidence thresholds allows GHGP to provide decision-useful, credible information that better aligns reported claims with real-world emissions outcomes, without relying on subjective, unscalable additionality constructs that have historically limited the usefulness of project accounting.

answers.label: Regions warranting different tests, with examples
answers.text:
I answered “no” under the proposed framework. However, regional differences should be reflected in the baseline emissions scenario, specifically through differences in existing grid resources (OM) and likely new capacity additions (BM).

Under MIM, the baseline scenario provides the reference case against which the emissions impact of an action is estimated. As the Project Protocol notes, “distinguishing a project activity from its baseline scenario is often referred to as determining additionality” (PP, p. 16). In this context, baseline-setting, rather than binary additionality testing, is the appropriate mechanism to reflect regional differences (see activities described in response to Q. 30 #2).

Consumption emissions impact refers to the GHG emissions caused by consumption at a specific location and time, calculated using marginal EFs, relative to a baseline scenario in which the load doesn’t exist. Procurement emissions impact refers to the electric-sector GHG emissions avoided or caused by generation or storage projects at a specific location and time, also based on marginal EFs.

Using a standardized methodology based on accessible, historical data, applied consistently to both consumption and procurement, provides cost-effective and decision-useful information. It also limits risks of gaming and inappropriate comparisons between consequential avoided emissions and attributional LB inventories.

Consistent with Project accounting principles, marginal EFs represent a production-based standard with dynamic baseline emission rates that change over time to provide a consistent methodology for similar project activities without the need to identify individual baseline scenarios. These dynamic baselines reflect displaced generation sources capable of providing the same product where baseline candidates are expected to change as grid conditions change (PP, pp. 14–15).

The Protocol explicitly recognizes that baseline candidates and emission rates may shift significantly over time and that dynamic baselines improve environmental integrity by keeping estimates accurate and aligned with changing circumstances (PP, p. 21). A multi-project baseline or benchmark can be used to estimate emissions for similar activities, avoiding the need to define a custom-made baseline for every project (PP, p. 13). The primary effect of an activity may include production and consumption and is defined as a change relative to baseline emissions (PP, p. 11).

As a result, the same action can have significantly different emissions impacts across locations and time periods. Unlike MBM, where a reporter may report zero emissions for the duration of a CFE contract, the marginal emissions impact of consumption, generation, or storage projects will change over time as grid conditions evolve.

Project economics also vary significantly by region. What has been built and what’s likely to be built is reflected in the baseline. Uncommon or first-of-a-kind technologies will often require long-term off-take agreements and may be appropriately included on a Positive List.

Finally, as grids decarbonize, demonstrating impact under MIM will become more challenging. Build margins will decline more rapidly as clean resources dominate new capacity additions, and operating margins will eventually fall as clean resources are on the margin more frequently. In such contexts, MIM could help encourage reporters in an already clean grid (e.g., Norway) to take actions beyond their local market.

Regional differences therefore are reflected in the baseline emissions scenario. Using dynamic, location- and time-specific marginal EFs based on observable historical data ensures that the same action can yield different impacts depending on where and when it occurs. This approach maintains consistency and integrity while recognizing project economics, grid mix, and decarbonization pathways vary significantly across regions and over time.

answers.label: Claims possible under different test approaches
answers.text:
Tests should be standardized. Claims should be tailored to the tests passed (see responses to Q. 30 & Q. 42). Impact accounting must be purpose-driven, as no single metric or accounting rule can serve all functions. It should provide accurate, decision-useful information to support corporate target-setting, where quantification methods and data ensure claims are properly aligned with the reported data.

GHGP isn't a target-setting body, but accounting should provide sufficient information to support corporate target-setting. Otherwise, it’ll be functionally useless. While recognition programs can decide which elements of a GHG report to use to meet targets, if key information is omitted, then the relevance and scientific integrity of reporting will be compromised.

Accounting should recognize the diversity of company goals, market access, and regional circumstances, and enable a wide range of climate-beneficial actions. A “one-size fits all” procurement strategy won’t work. Multiple factors may affect whether projects exist so binary additionality tests may not always apply. Therefore, a comprehensive multi-statement GHG report is needed to incentivize companies to make impactful investments in lower carbon products, projects and actions; enable investors to better evaluate a company’s decarbonization efforts; and empower customers to make informed procurement and consumption choices that support their climate objectives.

Impact-related disclosures can serve multiple purposes and support different types of claims.

1) Key Impact Indicators:

Objective, verifiable metrics (e.g., new or incremental CFE, life extensions, long-term PPAs, on-site generation) that are easy to measure, communicate, and link to decarbonization actions.

2) Impact Relative to a Standardized Baseline:

Helps identify which EACs or actions have meaningful climate benefits, guiding decisions on where, when, and what technologies to deploy, and incentivizing reductions in grid-level emissions.

• Impact estimates can reveal information not disclosed in inventories, recognizing that not all EACs have the same climate benefit.
• In some instances, impact estimates may not always be directly tied to an additionality claim (e.g., deciding where economic CFE should be located, how to comply with policy mandates, how to operate existing storage, or the effect of comingled public/private support).
• Impact estimates could be used to incentivize organizations to minimize the negative grid-level impact of their consumption.
• Procurement impact may be independent from the timing, location, and quantity of a reporter’s consumption.
• For completeness, accounting should include both positive and negative GHG effects. Excluding negative impacts will threaten the relevance of reported inventories (e.g., a company could add new fossil generation to serve new load, match it with existing EACs, and not report grid-level impacts).

3) Causality/Additionality Tests:

Should support stronger causal claims for certified projects, but qualitative or overly restrictive tests should be avoided to maintain accessibility and applicability across reporters. Consistent with the theory of change underlying Scope 2 MBM (Guidance, p. 89), all users should retain “baseline access” to clean electricity, while increasingly supporting advanced buyers to access and structure more robust climate actions. Additional “nice to have” labels provide more context so that users and stakeholders have the information necessary to make appropriate and informed decisions with reasonable confidence as to the integrity of the reported information.

Impact accounting should provide layered, actionable, and standardized information that differentiates between actions (affecting grid level emissions), cause (actions caused by a reporter), and effects (calculated differences from the baseline), supports target-setting, and ensures the integrity and relevance of GHG reporting.

answers.label: Details on operating margin methodologies
answers.text:
Consequential accounting is intended to capture grid realities (i.e., the marginal impact on the grid from changes in generation and/or consumption at a specific time and place). Appropriate operating margin (OM) EFs are calculated using methods that identify which generators respond to load or generation changes. Since CFE resources with no or relatively low fuel costs generally operate whenever they’re available, average EFs typically mask the emissions associated with fossil generation that ramp down or up (i.e., under-estimating the negative emissions impact of new load or positive benefits of EE).

Use of grid operator security-constrained economic dispatch (SCED) analysis should be preferred. It directly captures which units change output by capturing fuel switching, congestion, ramping constraints, and start-up emissions. Grid operators rely on SCED to establish locational marginal price (LMP) signals that form the foundation of competitive electricity markets. LMPs serve as an important benchmark for investment, operating and consumption decisions. The goal should be to achieve sufficient accuracy to enable users and stakeholders to make appropriate and informed decisions with reasonable confidence as to the integrity of the reported information.

In circumstances where SCED results aren’t publicly available, statistical estimation using historical data grounded in observed dispatch can also capture real-world system behavior without full simulation and forward-looking assumptions. But such models would need to be updated frequently to reflect dynamic structural changes over time.

Calculating capacity factor OM, based on the generation-weighted EF of marginal generators most available to ramp up or down (e.g., using EPA’s eGRID non-baseload EFs, CDM’s “simple OM” approach of using all generating power plants except low operating cost/must-run units, or the “average load-following” approach for Grid-Connected Projects) is conceptually aligned with MIM. While these methods are better than using simple average EFs, they’re less rigorous and less accurate.

GHGP should provide clear guidance on how organizations quantify and separately disclose the marginal emissions impact of a reporter’s consumption and procurement activities using a standardized approach based on accessible (public, free, and credible) data. Although forward-looking modeling may be appropriate for internal company decision-making, routine external disclosures of marginal emissions impacts should rely on historical operating margin EF data derived from observable system outcomes. Regular reporting of marginal emissions impact over time will encourage reporters to account for both current and future impacts of their consumption and procurement decisions.

Relying on observable data, rather than model assumptions and scenarios of highly uncertain future outcomes, allows for increased accuracy of reporting and limits gaming opportunities. Use of consistent methodologies is necessary to allow for meaningful comparisons of GHG emissions for the company over time or across companies. Companies shouldn’t calculate marginal OM or BM EFs associated with grid-connected electricity on their own but instead utilize publicly accessible data from standardized data sources that comply with the GHG Protocol. While paid or non-public data sources could be permitted under limited circumstances, their use shouldn’t be required.

The OM EFs shall be based on the location and timing of consumption and the location and timing of generation. Unlike MBM, even if both consumption and generation occur within the same grid and at the same time, these EFs could differ due to transmission congestion. However, any consumption and generation occurring at the exact same time and place should be assigned the same marginal EFs. The same EF hierarchy/decisions should be applied for both consumption and procurement projects.

answers.label: Details on build margin methodologies
answers.text:
Limiting the applicability of BM emissions impacts solely to renewable energy projects, as implied in Q.38, is inappropriate (see response to Q.30, #2). BM impacts should apply symmetrically across technologies and actions that affect future capacity outcomes, not be restricted by project type.

Use of recent capacity additions is the most appropriate methodology. Reliance on empirical, historical data, rather than forward-looking models, improves accuracy, transparency, and comparability, while reducing the risk of gaming. A standardized, post-hoc approach grounded in observable outcomes is better suited for routine GHG reporting.

By contrast, capacity expansion models aren’t appropriate for reliable, consistent and accurate GHG reporting. These models depend heavily on subjective assumptions about future prices, policies, technology costs, and system needs, and routinely produce divergent results even when applied contemporaneously by experienced practitioners. While such models may inform internal planning or investment decisions, forecasting uncertain, long-term counterfactual outcomes shouldn’t be the basis for emissions reporting. Like financial reporting, GHG accounting should focus on observable facts from prior periods, recognizing that past performance doesn’t guarantee future results.

For baseline candidate GHG emission rates to be credible, transparency regarding their derivation is essential (PP, p. 67). When identifying baseline candidates, the Project Protocol suggests starting with a temporal range that includes recently built plants, equipment, or recently established practices (PP, p. 44). Common practice refers to the predominant technologies or practices in a given market, as determined by the degree to which those technologies or practices have penetrated the market (defined by a specified geographic area). For example, in one area a certain technology may have a 60 percent market share, while in another area it may only have a 15 percent market share (PP, p. 45-46). In the baseline procedure, the baseline candidates include individual plants, instances of a technology, or practices that provide the same product or service as the project activity at that location and time. For example, electricity can be produced using a variety of generation technologies that rely on different fuels. For a project activity whose product is electricity production, the baseline corresponds to all fuel types and technologies used by the baseline candidates (PP, p. 66).

The Guidelines for Grid Connected Electricity Projects and UNFCCC use the emissions rate of the 20% of generation from the most recently constructed capacity in a grid region to determine a post-hoc BM. The BM should be calculated using a standardized methodology based on the average emissions rate associated with the generation from the specific plants built to serve the last 20% of load. This approach provides a reasonable proxy for the types of resources likely to serve incremental load. The same methodology can be extended to calculate time-differentiated (e.g., hourly) build margins, reflecting how capacity additions vary by time of day and system needs. BM values will and should vary significantly by grid region based on underlying economic and system conditions.

By grounding BM emissions impacts in observed capacity additions and applying them consistently across technologies, the proposed approach advances GHGP’s core principles, delivering credible, comparable, and implementable impact information without undermining integrity or feasibility. It preserves integrity by grounding EFs in what actually occurred, rather than speculative projections. It ensures reporters apply the same rules when estimating BM impacts. Reliance on publicly accessible, historical data minimizes reporting burden, avoids requiring companies to develop or procure complex proprietary models, and supports scalability.

answers.label: Assessing model applicability to project types
answers.text:
GHGP potentially could adopt a standardized, geography-agnostic methodology for weighting OM and BM impacts that depend on project types (see alternative proposal in response to Q. 51) with outcomes driven by observable project characteristics and regional system conditions, not discretionary methodological choices. Differences in results would arise from regional OM/BM EFs and the nature of the intervention, not from reporter-specific assumptions.

A standardized approach should:
1. Reflect likely power system responses over time, distinguishing between short-run dispatch impacts (OM) and longer-run capacity impacts (BM);
2. Be reproducible and consistent across reporters, enabling comparability;
3. Avoid subjectivity and gaming by relying on observable, historical data;
4. Preserve feasibility, particularly for smaller actors.

Role of Hourly OM/BM EFs:

Hourly OM and BM emission factors capture differences in generation mix, load shape, and technology availability, enabling consistent treatment of diverse production and consumption patterns. The timing (shape) and availability (capacity or load factor) of actual generation or consumption should be reflected within a standardized OM/BM baseline methodology (see responses to Q. 40, Q. 37, and Q. 32).

The relationship between OM and BM varies by region and time, reflecting market structure, policy constraints, and stage of transition. OM and BM can change independently:

• Early-transition, fossil-dominant regions: OM high ≈ BM high → short- and long-term impacts broadly align.
• Transitioning or policy-constrained regions: OM moderate–high > BM low → OM reflects legacy fossil dispatch, while new capacity is cleaner or policy-driven.
• Mature, high-clean-penetration regions: OM low or near zero < BM uncertain → incremental load may drive new firm fossil capacity even when OM appears low.

As grids decarbonize, BM typically declines faster than OM, creating prolonged periods where OM > BM. Using OM alone can overstate long-term impacts, while using BM alone can understate near-term impacts. The OM/BM gap itself is a meaningful signal of transition dynamics. (e.g., OM can be expected to be higher in regions where fossil generation is often on the margin (MISO, PJM) and BM to be relatively lower in regions with high RE development (ERCOT, MISO, then CAISO)).

Standardized Applicability Screens for OM/BM Weighting:

GHGP could require reporters to apply uniform screens to determine how OM and BM are weighted, without altering the underlying methodology.

A. Project Size: Large projects or aggregated actions with the potential to influence dispatch or investment require rigor and explicit OM/BM treatment. De minimis projects may rely on standardized OM/BM factors where system impacts are unlikely to be material.

B. Project Shape (Temporal Profile): Peaked, time-specific, or dispatchable actions (e.g., storage, demand response) require hourly OM/BM treatment. Flat or predictable profiles may permit aggregated application if temporal coincidence is demonstrated.

C. Dispatchability and Availability: Variable, low-capacity factor resources (e.g., solar, wind) must reflect when output occurs and what’s displaced. High availability resources may allow aggregation, provided location and timing alignment with EFs are shown.

Transparency and Claim Integrity:

For transparency and comparability, reporters should be required to disclose project characteristics triggering application of the standardized OM/BM approach and whether the resulting estimates are suitable for impact estimation versus causal or additionality claims (see responses to Q. 30, Q. 34 and Q. 42).

This approach allows GHGP to maintain a single, standardized methodology; reflect grid behavior across regions and transition stages; avoid subjective additionality determinations; and enable scalable, decision-useful impact reporting aligned with both short- and long-term decarbonization outcomes.

answers.label: Other appropriate emission rates or metrics
answers.text:
GHGP doesn’t need to set targets or grade performance, but it must enable complete, transparent accounting and reporting that distinguishes a wide range of climate actions and outcomes. Without this, the Scope 2 update risks losing credibility and will fail the practical “laugh test.”

GHGP accounting should allow users to clearly distinguish between “exceptional” climate leadership and “ugly” outcomes, even when both may appear similar in inventory disclosures.

Illustrative Outcomes—

Exceptional (Directly change what’s built, operated, or retired; reduce marginal grid-level emissions; cause durable system effects that wouldn’t likely occur otherwise):
• Enable first-of-a-kind or emerging firm and flexible CFE (advanced nuclear, geothermal, long duration storage)
• Sign LT PPAs that enable new firm or renewable CFE in constrained or fossil-heavy regions
• Support early retirement of fossil capacity with enforceable closure commitments
• Fund transmission that unlocks CFE interconnection
• Implement permanent EE that reduces peak demand
• Design data centers or industrial loads for 24/7 hourly CFE matching
• Pair electrification with CFE charging
• Take significant voluntary actions beyond regulatory requirements.

Good (Support clean energy demand or improve use of clean energy, even if causal impact is limited):
• Purchase EACs from incremental resources
• Select locations and technologies that maximize impact when complying with mandates (e.g., RPS)
• Site and switch load to where and when clean resources are marginal
• Switch to lower-carbon or green products
• Purchase EACs from existing clean resources (okay).

Bad (Increase emissions through design choices, neglect, or incomplete accounting):
• Add new load served by fossil generation without accounting for marginal impacts, while relying on average LB EFs or legacy MB EACs to mask emissions
• Match fossil-served new load with non-deliverable, existing EACs in transmission-constrained regions (e.g., NYC load matched with upstate NY EACs)
• Operate storage in ways that increase system emissions
• Promote electrification without managed charging in fossil-heavy grids.

Ugly (Directly cause durable, new fossil emissions, while claiming CFE use):
• Build or contract long-term new fossil supply to serve incremental load, while claiming 100% CFE use through legacy, SSS, or existing-resource EACs
• Extend the life of existing coal plants to serve new load.

GHGP has appropriately established distinct and complementary roles for inventory and consequential accounting. This distinction is essential since climate outcomes depend on what changes on the grid, not solely on how emissions are allocated within an inventory.

Proposed Metrics for Complete Reporting:

There’s broad expert consensus that decarbonization requires:

• Delivering CFE to consumption reliably and affordably while supporting economic growth & electrification,
• Extending the operating lives of existing CFE,
• Adding diverse incremental CFE & balancing resources, and
• Prioritizing actions that reduce actual grid-level emissions.

GHG accounting must measure what matters, enabling users to manage toward these outcomes. In addition to LB and MB inventories, GHGP should require disclosure of complementary, objective metrics. E.g.,

• CFE Score (%)
• Average inventory intensities
• Consumption level & % change
• EAC mix (% of consumption):
o Incremental/new resources
o New emerging technologies
o Firm/balancing
o Long-term PPAs
o On-site generation
o Legacy contracts
o SSS
• Procurement emissions impact (PEI)
• Consumption emissions impact (CEI)
• Impact ratio: PEI/CEI (without target setting).

Viewed together, these metrics provide a more accurate, decision-useful, and complete picture of company actions and their real-world effects. They allow claims to be aligned with disclosed evidence, support diverse decarbonization pathways, and preserve GHGP’s role as an accounting, policy-neutral, framework.

answers.label: Why that spatial granularity ceiling
answers.text:
The maximum appropriate level of spatial granularity for marginal EFs is the smallest geographic area over which dispatch and investment decisions are actually coordinated and observable, subject to data accessibility and feasibility constraints.

In practice, OM impacts are most accurately measured at nodal or zonal (LMP-based) levels, where such data are accessible. Dispatch decisions respond to local congestion and system constraints, and consequential impacts can therefore vary significantly over relatively small geographic areas. Nodal granularity provides the highest precision and credibility for OM impacts and allows consequential accounting to reflect transmission congestion within market boundaries, an important distinction from MBM.

BM impacts, by contrast, should be measured at the balancing authority, ISO/RTO market, or large sub-regional level in large markets. Capacity investment decisions are coordinated at these system scales, not at nodal or zonal levels. Measuring BM at finer spatial resolutions would misrepresent how investment decisions are actually made and introduce unnecessary subjectivity.

The appropriate level of granularity ultimately depends on what data are publicly accessible, credible, and reproducible. Similar to the proposed updates for the LB inventory, a nested spatial-temporal hierarchy should apply:

• Reporters shall use the most precise spatial boundary for which high-quality EF data are accessible.
• Within that spatial boundary, reporters shall use the most precise temporal granularity available.
• The selected EF must be the most appropriate, accurate, and highest-quality option available for the reporting purpose.

This approach aligns with the Project Protocol, which states that when baseline candidates are constrained by physical infrastructure, such as supply networks for electricity and fuels, the geographic extent of that infrastructure (i.e., the power grid for grid-connected electricity projects or relevant market boundary) is the appropriate spatial boundary (PP, p. 42). The same logic applies to islanded or off-grid microgrids, where baseline candidates are constrained by local infrastructure.

OM reflects emissions from existing generation displaced by changes in consumption or supply, and therefore varies by location, time, fuel type, and system conditions. BM reflects emissions associated with avoided or deferred capacity additions, which are determined by system-level planning and investment decisions. As grids evolve – through retirements, new builds, and transmission upgrades – both OM and BM will change over time and differ substantially across regions.

In short, OM should be as spatially granular as dispatch allows, while BM should reflect the geographic scale at which investment decisions are coordinated. This preserves accuracy, integrity, and feasibility while ensuring consequential impacts reflect real grid behavior rather than artificial or speculative boundaries.

answers.label: Why that temporal granularity ceiling
answers.text:
The appropriate temporal granularity depends on what credible, accessible spatial and temporal granular data are available (see response to Q. 44) and potentially by project type (see response to Q. 41). The selected EF must be the most appropriate, accurate, and highest-quality option available for the reporting purpose.

OM emissions can vary significantly over time depending on load levels, the types of power plants on the grid, and the order in which they are dispatched to meet load. In principle, sub-hourly (or hourly) granularity is the maximum appropriate level because dispatch, ramping, congestion, and marginal resource responses occur at sub-hourly intervals. This best preserves causal accuracy for OM impacts.

However, accuracy depends not just on resolution, but on how EFs are constructed. Well-constructed seasonal, monthly, TOU, daily, or hourly marginal rates derived from hourly dispatch data can still be causally valid if they preserve marginal signals without distortion (i.e., the difference between a simple average and “average marginal” approach discussed in the Guidelines for Grid-Connected Electricity Projects).

For example, electricity market prices can be “accurate” over different time periods if they reflect market prices for the relevant time and location, preserve economic signals, and aggregate or disaggregate without distortion when changing time resolution. E.g., a reasonably accurate TOU rate can be constructed based on hourly LMP data and load profiles to encourage more efficient use of the electric grid, trading off accuracy with usability.

Currently, the marginal emissions impact of a reporter’s consumption or procurement actions aren’t estimated directly in either LB or MB inventories. Therefore, improvement, not perfection, should be the near-term goal. The underlying methodologies, data and rigor of calculations that may be used today can be improved and perfected over time. There’s broad agreement that more granular data can provide a more accurate climate impact assessment and that consequential electric-sector impacts can vary substantially by time of day and time of year. A reporter could begin to quantitatively estimate emissions impact beginning with relatively less complex calculations with readily available data (e.g., using EPA’s most recent AVERT annual avoided CO2 emissions factor). Nevertheless, the imperative of focusing on decarbonization impact suggests that we begin to require such disclosures as soon as possible and with the best available data and methodologies.

Stakeholders increasingly expect the Protocol to support estimation of actual emissions impacts and to help distinguish actions that meaningfully reduce emissions. The Protocol has been criticized for failing to connect inventory disclosures with real-world emissions outcomes. As a result, maintaining the status quo – characterized by non-standardized, non-prioritized, non-target-ready impact metrics – would undermine the GHGP’s relevance, credibility, and scientific integrity.

answers.label: Why selected weighting approaches are appropriate
answers.text:
When considering alternative weighting methods, there’s an inherent tradeoff between accuracy and usability.

Alternative Weighting Methods:
1) Fixed weighting (50/50)
2) Project type (RE, storage, EE, DR, load growth)
3) Region specific (grid transition stage, chronic excess/shortage of capacity)
4) Project specific (size, capacity factor, shape, dispatchability)
5) Model derived (historical analysis or forward capacity expansion)
6) Time varying (OM-heavy short-term, BM-heavy long-term).

Initially, a single standardized weighting of OM/BM (e.g., 50/50) could be applied across all electricity projects. It’s simple and transparent, highly comparable, low gaming risk, feasible to scale, and consistent with the Guidelines for Quantifying GHG Reductions from Grid-Connected Electricity Projects, which recommend a default 50/50 weighting where project-specific differentiation isn’t feasible. Alternative weighting frameworks (see response to Q. 51) can improve accuracy, but sacrifice comparability, feasibility/scalability and increase gaming risks.

A standardized, weighted OM/BM framework with conservative defaults informed by empirical evidence is the only approach that can scale, avoid gaming, and maintain GHGP’s credibility while still improving climate-impact relevance. A practical path forward is to start with a fixed default to ensure feasibility and comparability. Then use empirical research to validate or adjust defaults. Limited differentiation for clearly defined project types can be allowed, but project-specific weighting should be reserved for exceptional cases or supplemental disclosures with the weights used also being disclosed.

Further research may inform whether differentiated default weights by project type are warranted. Ongoing research by a coalition including VERACI-T, Climate TRACE, and ZEROgrid is directly relevant to informing GHGP’s final approach. This work is based on the premise that the combined BM and OM impact should approximate the total emissions impact of an intervention. Specifically, the research:

• Compiles data on a wide range of historical interventions that change net electricity demand or supply;
• Tests whether models using BM and OM weights can accurately predict observed changes in total emissions over subsequent years; and
• Validates whether the models correctly capture key causal drivers, such as the proportion of incremental generation met by newly built capacity versus existing resources.

This analysis evaluates historical emissions outcomes over multiple years and decades. Additional research also assesses the consistency of these results with capacity expansion model projections.

It’s expected that additional findings will be available prior to publication of GHGP’s final rules, which may support refinement or adjustment of the default weights. Over time, it may become appropriate to introduce a schedule of differentiated default weights by project type, consistent with the framework outlined in GHGP Guidelines for Quantifying GHG Reductions from Grid-connected Electricity Projects.

However, any increase in project-specific accuracy should be carefully weighed against the Protocol’s core objectives of consistency, comparability, and feasibility – as well as other accounting alternatives. For example, relative to the status quo, a simple, transparent default weighting approach is preferable and appropriate for initial implementation, with the option to evolve as data availability and methodological confidence improve.

In fact, staged improvements were made during the development of U.S. competitive electricity markets. Energy-only markets (LMP) were developed first (e.g., 1998 in PJM), followed by the creation of capacity markets (e.g., PJM’s daily capacity market in 1999 and then reliability pricing model redesign effective in 2007). Capacity markets were developed later only in some cases to supplement and further encourage long-term investment in resources.

answers.label: Weighting approaches not feasible to implement
Why selected weighting approaches are infeasible
answers.text:
A transparent, comparable and consistent standardized methodology for establishing OM and BM weights is needed that can scale, avoid gaming, and maintain GHGP’s credibility while improving the climate-impact relevance of GHG reporting.

Currently, the marginal emissions impact of a reporter’s consumption or procurement actions aren’t estimated directly in either LB or MB inventories. Therefore, improvement, not perfection, should be the near-term goal. The underlying methodologies, data and rigor of calculations that may be used today can be improved and perfected over time. Stakeholders increasingly expect the Protocol to support estimation of actual emissions impacts and to help distinguish actions that meaningfully reduce emissions. The Protocol has been criticized for failing to connect inventory disclosures with real-world emissions outcomes. As a result, maintaining the status quo – characterized by non-standardized, non-prioritized, non-target-ready impact metrics – would undermine the GHGP’s relevance, credibility, and scientific integrity.

In my view, the approaches that meet governance and credibility requirement are: 1) default 50/50 OM-BM weighting, 2) a standardized version of the existing GHGP Grid-Connected Electricity Guidelines framework, potentially informed by CDM Tool07 weighting criteria, or 3) an alternative proposal like described in response to Q. 51. While more complex approaches may improve theoretical accuracy, they mail fail the scalability, comparability, and gaming-risk criteria required for a global GHG accounting standard.

UNFCCC CDM Tool07 was designed for project-level baseline setting, not for system-wide, decision-driven consequential attribution. While its BM and OM concepts are directionally useful, several structural gaps (e.g., the lack of temporal matching of generation with displaced marginal units; less tied to grid surplus/shortage conditions) prevent it from being applied for consequential weighting today in a standardized manner.

Resource adequacy approaches (e.g., weighting based on capacity value, ELCC, planning reserve margins) aren’t suitable for standardized GHG reporting. They’re useful for planning studies, not for protocol-level accounting. They require deep, region-specific grid modeling and confidential utility planning data. While used by grid operators, translating these into a simple weighting factor framework isn’t scalable.

Intervention lifecycle approaches (e.g., modeling full lifetime effects of an action on dispatch and investment) are scientifically interesting but operationally unworkable. Assessing the lifecycle of an intervention requires complex, long-term grid forecasting. They are incompatible with GHGP’s need for transparency, consistency, credibility, comparability, and scalability, and are associated with high gaming risk.

A good weighting approach for a GHGP standard must bridge the gap between rigid simplicity and the high-accuracy (but low-feasibility) requirements of complex power system modeling. A robust approach should be rule-based, dynamic, objective, scalable, consistent, and resistant to gaming.

answers.label: Other approaches for assigning margin weights
answers.text:
To develop a standardized weighting methodology that’s consistent, scalable, and resistant to gaming, GHGP should adopt a rule-based approach that reflects how power systems respond to specific types of interventions. This ensures that outcomes are driven by regional EFs and project types rather than reporter discretion.

Proposed Weighting Framework:

1. Classify Project System Effects: Resource characteristics (such as dispatchability, intermittency, firm) affect when emissions are displaced (OM) and whether capacity investment decisions are affected (BM). Observable attributes can inform project classification and default OM/BM weighting, not the underlying EF calculation.

• OM-Dominant (Short-Term Dispatch):
o Intermittent/non-dispatchable resources where OM impact depends on when output occurs (limited BM unless paired with storage)
o Dispatchable / operationally flexible resources (storage) that primarily substitute for marginal fossil during high EF hours (depends on how resource is operated).

• BM-Dominant (Long-Term Capacity):
o Large new loads, transmission projects, fossil retirements, or firm resources aligned with peak demand
o On-peak interventions.

2. Apply Universal Persistence & Size Screens: Actions are considered more BM-relevant if at least 2 observable conditions are met:
• Duration: ≥ 5 yrs
• Predictability: contracted or operationally persistent/firm
• Size: ≥ 100 MW or ≥ 1% of regional peak load.

3. Assign Standardized Default Weights (OM%/BM%):
• High BM Impact (25/75 end state): New large anchor loads or dispatchable firm power (strong investment signal)
• Default (50/50): BAU load or no specific project data
• Low BM Impact (75/25): Intermittent resources (wind/solar), small-scale TOU shifts, or non-persistent load changes.
Consistent with UNFCCC CDM Tool guidance, no single weight exceeds 75% in the initial years.

4. Add Temporal Phasing for Long-Duration BM Actions
To reflect real-world investment dynamics where dispatch effects are immediate but capacity displacement takes time, weights should shift over a pre-set schedule & impact horizon. E.g.:
• Years 1-3 (75/25): immediate dispatch effects
• Years 4-6 (50/50): 1st deferrable investment effects
• Years 7-15 (25/75 or 50/50): capacity & retirement effects reach end state depending on project type.
The schedule may be accelerated for grids with chronic under-capacity or slowed for those with high reserve margins.

“Typically, the near-term impact of a CDM electricity project will largely be on the operation of power plants (OM) until the time of the first deferrable capacity additions…After some time, however, the CDM project activity should begin to affect a delay, displacement, or other modification of new capacity additions, and from there onwards, build margin effects should predominate” (CDM, Methodology Panel, Annex 8, p. 1).

5. Require Disclosures: To preserve transparency and comparability, reporters should disclose action classification, persistence and scale test results, OM and BM EFs used, time horizon and resulting blended EF.

6. Apply Uniform Methodology to Procurement & Consumption Actions: To ensure scientific integrity, the weighting rules must apply identically to both sides of the ledger. A standardized weighting approach would apply the same rules everywhere, avoid gaming with observable project classification thresholds, yet allow differentiated weights based on the type of intervention.

Key Outcomes:
• Comparability: Uniform global rules ensure a level playing field
• Credibility: Anchored in observed system behavior and CDM precedent
• Feasibility: Requires no complex modeling; relies on observable data
• Integrity: Resistant to gaming using fixed thresholds and observable data
• Relevance: Captures both short- and long-term emissions effects.

Emission impact estimates would complement but not replace inventories, preserving GHGP’s accounting framework while materially improving climate-impact relevance.

answers.label: Research supporting the suggested approach
answers.text:
GHGP and CDM already provide guidance for combining OM/BM. Their weighting is explicitly part of the combined margin calculation. Having a 50/50 default is common but alternative weights have been suggested when justified by project type. Practitioner frameworks and research confirm the importance of both short-term (dispatch) and long-run (capacity) components in credible emissions impact estimation.

This methodology follows the framework established in the UNFCCC Clean Development Mechanism’s (CDM) “Tool to Calculate the EF for an Electricity System,” which defines OM and BM EFs and calculates a weighted CM as part of baseline emissions estimation.

Recent implementations use a 50/50 weighting of OM and BM to represent both ST dispatch effects and LT capacity effects. Past practice under CDM has used 50% OM / 50% BM weights as a default, but alternative weights have been applied when technically justified, coupled with a suggestion not to exceed 75% during the first crediting period. https://cdm.unfccc.int/methodologies/PAmethodologies/tools/am-tool-07-v7.0.pdf, pp. 27-29.
https://climateactiontransparency.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/Renewable-Energy-Methodology_appendices.pdf, Appendix D.

Granular Registry’s “Long Run Marginal Emissions Rate” explicitly combines OM and BM as defined in the GHG Protocol project accounting standard, with a 50/50 weighting to reflect both ST dispatch and LT capacity effects. “The registry adopts the standard GHG Protocol weighting of 50% Operating Margin (OM) and 50% Build Margin (BM), providing a balanced perspective that accurately reflects both immediate dispatch impacts and future capacity expansions induced by incremental generation or load… Clear methodological guidelines ensure all stakeholders understand precisely how emissions rates are derived…The standardized 50/50 weighting and fallback monthly average ensure the approach remains globally scalable and implementable across diverse regions, even when current-year data is limited.” https://docs.granular-foundation.org/methodology/carbon-impact/assigning-long-run-marginal-emissions-rate

CDM guidance interprets the OM/BM combined margin as evolving: dispatch first, then capacity later, with explicit recommendations about how weighting should logically change across crediting periods. The CDM Meth Panel suggested shifting default weights from OM toward BM over successive crediting periods to reflect evolving impacts on emissions. “Typically, the near-term impact of a CDM electricity project will largely be on the operation of power plants (OM) until the time of the first deferrable capacity additions. … After some time, however, the CDM project activity should begin to affect a delay, displacement, or other modification of new capacity additions, and from there onwards, build margin effects should predominate.” CDM Preliminary Guidance for OM/BM Weighting, Annex 8, 18th Meeting, https://cdm.unfccc.int/Panels/meth/meeting/05/Meth18_repan8_OMBM.pdf, p. 1.

Grid-connected electricity project guidelines also suggest that emissions impacts can occur at different timescales (e.g., from existing units initially (OM) and from capacity deferral later (BM)), implying time dependence in relative margins.

The EPA recognizes that for many interventions, existing generator emissions are avoided in the short term (2–5 years), but larger or longer term projects also affect new units. “For most energy efficiency program activity in the US, it is safe to assume that only existing generator emissions are avoided in the short term of two to five years. However, if the analysis is estimating impacts over a longer period of time and/or the scale of the programs being evaluated is large enough, then new units could be considered as well.” (Model Energy Efficiency Program Impact Evaluation Guide, https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2015-08/documents/evaluation_guide.pdf, 11/2007, p. 82.)
